observation: He describes birthdays as persistently miserable and recalls childhood isolation before announcing a scheme to force people to attend.
reviewer_note: Reported memories and present motivation support distress. The absurd flashback is narrative evidence, not independently verified biography.

observation: He describes a repeated birthday problem but expects his new device to prevent another lonely birthday.
reviewer_note: Recurring distress does not establish that he believes relief is impossible; his attempted solution also does not prove that he feels free of suffering.

observation: His response to loneliness includes threatening Perry and planning to compel a crowd to celebrate with him.
reviewer_note: The explicit link between painful birthdays and coercive action weighs against managing this emotion constructively. Villainy alone would not establish poor regulation.

observation: After the Slave-inator falls, bystanders report an urge to clean up and start doing so.
reviewer_note: Consistent with the cleanup function described at lines 94-96; the short transcript does not describe the mechanism or establish general reliability.

observation: His machine fires at the Moon and rotates it; the attached building moves with it.
reviewer_note: The described mechanical effect succeeds even though his larger plan fails. Confidence concerns the transcript observation, not physical plausibility.

observation: He introduces a device designed to rotate the Moon.
reviewer_note: An unusual idea is compatible with originality, but this passage provides no comparison with prior inventions. Self-praise does not prove novelty.

observation: He expects rotating the Moon to remove the full moon, then notices the failure and recognizes reflected sunlight before proposing rotating the Sun.
reviewer_note: His stated causal model is mistaken, and the final proposal limits how much credit the correction deserves.

observation: He initially blames Perry, then changes his explanation when he recognizes that moonlight reflects sunlight.
reviewer_note: Some updating occurs, but his final proposal keeps the same flawed plan. This is partial flexibility, not a clean recovery.

observation: Perry performs household tasks for Doofenshmirtz and helps expose an intruder.
reviewer_note: The later flashback at lines 157-160 attributes the changed role to the Butler-inator; the effect is temporary and Perry defeats it.

observation: An accidental discharge from the Vaporizer-inator makes Cheesetopia evaporate.
reviewer_note: Shows a functioning effect within the story, but not successful targeting or control of the Tri-State Area.

observation: The Butler-inator combines a tailored outfit with an imposed servant identity and suppressed memory of fighting evil.
reviewer_note: This is a distinctive combination in the passage; no systematic comparison establishes novelty across the fictional world.

observation: After seeing the reminder Perry wrote before the memory change, Doofenshmirtz recognizes how a message to a future self defeats his plan.
reviewer_note: He recognizes the workaround after the event and admits he did not predict it. This is narrow retrospective insight.

observation: When a musical group unexpectedly crashes into his apartment, he welcomes the group and joins the dancing.
reviewer_note: A situational change of response is visible; enjoying the interruption does not establish durable adjustment or erase his coercive conduct elsewhere.

observation: His ray retrieves the ceremonial key; Perry then activates a return setting that releases the collected keys.
reviewer_note: Supports a functioning collection-and-return mechanism. The device later self-destructs, and the intended universal unlocking goal fails.

observation: Only after obtaining the oversized Key to the City does he question whether it is symbolic and too large for ordinary locks.
reviewer_note: He failed to check a central assumption before building his plan around it.

observation: After Perry destroys the machine, he initially shrugs it off and begins questioning the value of his prize.
reviewer_note: A brief restrained reaction supports situational regulation. The scene is cut short by lightning; sustained coping is unknown.

observation: He links his interest in keys to having been trapped in a cockroach-filled milk can for hours.
reviewer_note: The event sounds aversive, but this passage does not establish the intensity or persistence of present emotional suffering.

observation: Once Norm plugs in the Babe-inator, its beam turns Phineas and Ferb into babies.
reviewer_note: The transformation works in the narrative; it hits unintended targets and needs someone else to connect power.

observation: He interprets the inactive Babe-inator as another failed invention without noticing that it needs to be plugged in.
reviewer_note: An operational failure weighs against reliable problem solving; it does not erase the working design recorded in E18.

observation: After repeated perceived failures at evil, he applies to the agency and tries a new role working with Perry.
reviewer_note: A concrete change of goals and behavior occurs. E21 records its later reversal, so this is not treated as lasting reform.

observation: After being fired, he interprets criticism of the damage he caused as proof that he is good at evil and returns to it.
reviewer_note: He changes roles again but preserves his destructive goal rather than addressing the feedback. This is a qualified counterexample, not proof of zero adaptability.

observation: He treats repeated failure as a reason to try a different life and seeks employment at the agency.
reviewer_note: This shows a perceived alternative to his failing role. It is indirect evidence about inescapability of suffering, not proof of psychological well-being.

observation: He presents a vehicle that travels on water as his latest invention, calling it BO-AT.
reviewer_note: The joke describes rediscovering a familiar boat concept. This limits a blanket originality claim; it does not negate his other inventions.

observation: He accepts help from Perry and Monogram to find Vanessa, and father and daughter reconnect in Paris.
reviewer_note: He cooperates across the usual enemy relationship for his daughter. Her complaint about being put second remains part of the same scene; one reconciliation is not a permanent change.

observation: After the truth ray visibly affects others, a reflected shot makes him disclose that he is secretly very lonely.
reviewer_note: Within the story the ray makes the admission credible. Loneliness supports distress, but its duration and severity are unspecified.

observation: He blames Perry for all his failures and only grudgingly concedes responsibility after his solo attempt fails.
reviewer_note: Resistance to corrective evidence precedes the change later in this episode.

observation: Stranded and exhausted, he cries and repeatedly calls himself a failure before Perry brings tickets.
reviewer_note: An explicit episode of suffering and harsh self-judgment. Acute exhaustion contributes; this is not a diagnosis.

observation: He generalizes that failure has always been his fault, then accepts Perry’s help.
reviewer_note: Global self-blame suggests entrapment but does not explicitly say relief is impossible. Help changes his immediate response.

observation: After leaving Perry behind on a bus, he reconsiders, stops the bus, and returns with a jetpack to collect him.
reviewer_note: The behavior changes after reflection, beyond a verbal promise. His initial abandonment prevents reading the whole sequence as uncomplicated kindness.

observation: Positive memories of Vanessa interrupt his effort to accumulate painful memories and reduce the fictional meter reading.
reviewer_note: The ordinary framing of this clip show depicts access to positive experience. The meter is a plot device, not a clinical measure, and relief alone does not establish his beliefs about escape.

observation: After an embarrassing video becomes widely viewed, he says he will never live it down.
reviewer_note: Explicit language of lasting embarrassment supports a narrow perceived-inescapability reading. It may be comic exaggeration and does not establish permanent entrapment in all suffering.

observation: He admits a creative block, asks Perry for help, and participates in exercises that lead to a new design.
reviewer_note: He recognizes a limitation and changes his approach with another person’s help. His goal remains an evil scheme, so flexibility does not imply benevolence.

observation: When a falling tire destroys his new machine, he responds with a wry remark about his uncle’s saying.
reviewer_note: This immediate reaction shows tolerating a setback. It cannot establish regulation in other situations.

observation: His eye-examination technology is described as being used commercially, with royalties, and his new ray visibly blurs vision.
reviewer_note: Narrated use and depicted effects support effective application within the fictional world. Commercial details are partly his account.

observation: He receives royalties for technology used in eye-examination equipment.
reviewer_note: Adoption gives more context than a self-awarded invention name, but neither royalties nor adoption establishes novelty relative to prior designs.

observation: He describes Father’s Day as especially difficult and connects it with being forced to serve as a lawn gnome in childhood.
reviewer_note: The current emotional report matters here; the replayed childhood scene is not treated as a new independent event.

observation: He believes returning his father’s gnome could let them start again and heal old wounds.
reviewer_note: This directly expresses a possible route to improvement in a painful relationship. It does not show that the plan will work.

observation: His father compares the broken gift unfavorably with Roger’s, and Heinz leaves with his voice breaking in tears.
reviewer_note: Present suffering is depicted, beyond the remembered backstory.

observation: After the disappointing visit, he accepts Perry’s consolation, appreciates their relationship, and goes home.
reviewer_note: He acknowledges hurt and seeks connection without retaliating in this passage. Distress and regulation can occur together.

observation: He obtains Johnny’s hair as a DNA source and plans an antidote while organizing others to find Johnny.
reviewer_note: The passage links a biological input to a proposed solution within cartoon science. The later reversal supports the plan’s utility, not real-world scientific validity.

observation: The antidote restores Johnny after Vanessa administers it; Perry helps with the rescue.
reviewer_note: The substance works, but the delivery is accidental and the rescue is collective. This is not a solo or flawlessly executed success.

observation: In the future-set episode, he abandons the induced midlife crisis and chooses his familiar life and friends.
reviewer_note: This is the older Heinz, kept separate from ordinary summer events. He briefly proposes evil and accepts Perry’s correction; change is not flawless.

observation: He connects repeated events to activation of his Do-Over-inator and identifies the repeating day.
reviewer_note: A causal inference about the mechanism, supported by the ongoing loop narrative. Recognizing the loop does not mean he foresaw all its consequences.

observation: While absorbed in the repeating day, he ignores Vanessa’s attempt to discuss moving out.
reviewer_note: His initial priorities remain rigid. This is an earlier stage of the same time-loop episode, not a separate independent episode.

observation: When Vanessa challenges his commitment to being evil, he considers that he could become a good person.
reviewer_note: Her explanation about obligation to backstories is her interpretation. His own willingness to consider another life challenges an unqualified belief that he is trapped.

observation: In the next loop he recalls Vanessa’s wishes, vows to stop being evil, and asks her help to end the loops.
reviewer_note: He changes his goal in response to her needs. The later ending (E50) gives more weight than the vow alone.

observation: After another reset frustrates his attempt, he tears down a lamp and throws it at Norm.
reviewer_note: An enacted angry response persists even during his turn toward good. A constructive new goal is not equivalent to consistent regulation.

observation: Across shortened loops, he starts disclosing the device’s risks and asks Vanessa and Perry for agreement.
reviewer_note: He adjusts his approach and involves others. The numerical risks are his dialogue, not measured probabilities; repeated loops are one connected sequence.

observation: His activation and Candace’s destruction of the other device coincide with the end of the time loop.
reviewer_note: The outcome supports a contribution to a working solution. Two simultaneous actions prevent attributing the entire result to him alone.

observation: After time is restored, he remains committed to learning how to be good and accepts Vanessa’s help.
reviewer_note: The change carries beyond the erased loops. This is stronger evidence of development than a temporary plan, but not proof of lifelong stability.

observation: In OWCA agent training he says he has given up evil, while Carl says the trainees still need teamwork.
reviewer_note: The new role corroborates the reform direction. His statement and participation do not establish that he has mastered emotional regulation or teamwork.
